output.brief: The evidence doesn't support blaming the Admissions Office for the enrolment drop. Applications and admits rose, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield (admits who enrolled) fell about 7 points in both rounds. That includes early action, which was handled on the old system and on the usual schedule, so the late regular-decision answers can't explain most of the fall. The clearest pattern is by scholarship tier. Yield collapsed only in the Dean's tier (award cut from $14,000 to $9,000) and the Merit tier ($9,000 to $5,000). It held steady in the Presidential tier, where awards were unchanged, and among students with no merit award. The October 2025 award cut is the most likely cause, and the finance committee judged its yield effect on an outdated 2021 estimate. The slow regular-decision turnaround and the portal problems were real service failures, and they may have cost individual students, but they don't explain the overall drop. Replacing the director on this basis would punish the wrong party. Next steps: take the award schedule back to the finance committee with a modelled proposal for the affected tiers, and set a turnaround target. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until missing documents are verified. I'm fairly confident in the main conclusion. The size of the delay effect is uncertain.
